tests.weakness: location.hash flows into innerHTML and location.search into document.write; a signature-preview field renders victim-typed HTML locally (Self-DOM-XSS, sub-doc 01.1). A nonce-based CSP variant blocks the self-XSS payload while the default page has no CSP.

tests.surface: GET /js-exec?expr=&cb=, new Function / setTimeout(string) buttons, GET /api/jsonp?callback=
tests.weakness: eval(), new Function() and setTimeout(string) execute user input; the JSONP callback name is unsanitised so a callback of 'window.__jsonp_xss=1;//' runs arbitrary JS in the victim origin.

User markup is reflected unencoded under a script-src 'none' CSP: injected scripts are blocked but spoofed content, forms and iframes render, and an injected credential form submits to the attacker origin.
location.href is assigned the raw 'next' parameter with no allowlist and no scheme validation; navigation to the attacker origin and javascript: URLs are accepted by the sink.
User-controlled CSS is injected into a <style> block on a page holding a secret token; attribute selectors plus url() callbacks exfiltrate the token's characters to the in-range attacker listener.
The page loads a <script> (and iframe) whose src is taken straight from the URL, so attacker-controlled JS executes in the victim origin and reads its cookies.

Origin reflection with credentials, an unanchored prefix regex (http://127.0.0.1:8901 passes), an unanchored subdomain regex (trusted.lab.test.evil.com passes), Origin: null allowed with credentials, and ACAO:* on an unauthenticated PII endpoint. The attacker origin reads the victim's authenticated data in a real browser.
The state-changing transfer form sends no X-Frame-Options and no frame-ancestors; the attacker origin frames it under a decoy button and a click on the decoy fires the authenticated transfer.

tests.surface: WS /ws opened from the attacker origin
tests.weakness: The WebSocket handshake performs no Origin check and authenticates by cookie only (SameSite=None), so a cross-origin page opens an authenticated socket (CSWSH) and performs a transfer; message content is acted on and echoed without sanitisation.

tests.surface: GET /messages framed by the attacker origin, postMessage both directions
tests.weakness: The message receiver never validates event.origin and replies with targetOrigin '*': a cross-origin frame reads the victim's profile/CSRF token and triggers an authenticated email change.

tests.surface: GET /storage?note=, localStorage/sessionStorage/IndexedDB, storage events across tabs
tests.weakness: Session token, PII and card data are parked in localStorage, sessionStorage and IndexedDB; the page's DOM-XSS sink lets injected script read and exfiltrate them, and a storage-event handler propagates secrets to every other tab.

tests.surface: GET /api/private.js, /api/jsonp?callback=, /api/orders included via <script src> from the attacker origin
tests.weakness: Authenticated sensitive data is served as includable JavaScript (a global variable and a JSONP callback), so a cross-origin <script> inclusion reads it without CORS. A top-level-array endpoint for the historical Array-constructor hijack is also provided (modern browsers use the intrinsic Array, so that variant no longer fires - documented in README).
Links open with an explicit rel=opener (and window.open without noopener) and no COOP header; the opened attacker page navigates window.opener.location to a phishing page on the attacker origin.
User input is reflected raw into an AngularJS 1.8.2 template (expression sandbox removed in 1.8); {{constructor.constructor('...')()}} executes arbitrary JS in the victim origin.
The page reads window.config.href to choose a script src; an injected <a id=config href=attacker> clobbers the undefined global via named DOM access and loads attacker JS in the victim origin.

tests.surface: GET /dashboard framed cross-origin (window.length), GET /api/search?q= via <script> load/error events
tests.weakness: Two real cross-site oracles: the dashboard's iframe count reveals authentication state through cross-origin window.length, and 200-vs-404 on a private-note search lets an attacker page recover secret digits via script load/error events.

The client-side viewer concatenates user input into fetch('/api/files/'+doc); ../ segments are normalised by the browser into /api/admin/users, reaching an unintended endpoint that returns every user's PII.

An unauthenticated 'custom script' endpoint stores arbitrary same-origin JS served with Service-Worker-Allowed: /, and the page registers the URL-chosen script as a service worker with root scope; the worker intercepts and rewrites /api/data responses.

tests.surface: DNS rebind.lab.test (TTL 0) via :8953, Chromium through the :8908 rebinding proxy, http://rebind.lab.test:8902/
tests.weakness: The authoritative lab DNS flips rebind.lab.test between the attacker container IP and the internal victim container IP with TTL 0; the internal service accepts any Host without auth. A real Chromium page loaded from the attacker phase reads the internal secret same-origin after the flip (resolution delegated to the in-range proxy).
